note: A man left money in another's care. The guardian gave it to his mother, who put it in a chest, and it was stolen. Rava asked how judges should rule. The guardian cannot simply be ordered to pay, because anyone who leaves something in another's care knows that his family may look after it. The mother cannot be ordered to pay, because her son never told her the money was not his, or she would have buried it. And the son can say that letting her think it was his made her even more careful. Rava ruled that the son swears he gave it to his mother, she swears she put it in the chest and it was stolen, and the son is exempt.
why: The Gemara is gathering rulings on when a guardian of money is negligent, such as hiding it in a willow hut or forgetting where it is; this case asks whether handing it to a family member counts.

people.name: Rava
people.about: He works through each party's defense and rules on the case.

terms.meaning: Someone who agrees to look after another person's property and may have to pay if it is lost through negligence.
A solemn sworn statement in court, used to settle claims that cannot otherwise be proven.

flag: The STORY segments stop before Rava's ruling (oaths, guardian exempt), which falls in AFTER segment 9; the boundary probably should include it.

note: A guardian handling the affairs of orphans bought them an ox and handed it to a cowherd. The ox had no molars or teeth to eat with, and it died. Rami bar Hama asked how judges should rule. The guardian can say he gave it to the cowherd, and the cowherd can say he put it with the other oxen and threw it food, not knowing it did not eat. Since the orphans got their money back from the seller, the Gemara reasons, the claim comes from the seller, a trader who did not know of the defect: he swears he did not know, and the cowherd pays him the value of the meat at the cheapest price.
why: The Gemara is working through a run of cases in which property in someone's care passes through several hands and is lost, each asking how judges should rule; this one follows Rava's case of the guardian who gave money to his mother.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: The Sage who poses the question of how judges should rule.

terms.meaning: Someone paid to look after another's property; he must pay for losses caused by his lack of care.
A sale of an item with a hidden defect, which can be undone so the buyer gets his money back.
A person appointed to manage the property of orphans who are too young to manage it themselves.

note: A man left hops, used in making beer, in another's care. The guardian also had his own pile of hops, and he told his brewer to use hops from this pile, but the brewer went and used the other pile, the one left in his care. Rav Amram asked how judges should rule. The guardian can say he told the brewer which pile to use, and the brewer can say he was never told not to use the other one. The story itself does not give a ruling.
why: One of a run of cases in which property left in someone's care is lost through another person's hands; the discussion that follows asks whether the guardian is still to blame and what loss there really was.

people.name: Rav Amram
people.about: The Sage who poses the question of how judges should rule.

terms.meaning: A plant used in brewing beer.
Someone who agrees to look after another person's property and may have to pay if it is lost.

note: Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis disputed whether a certain oven could become impure. Losing the argument, he called on a carob tree, a stream and the study hall walls to prove him right; each did, and the Rabbis rejected each. A Divine Voice declared that the law follows him, yet Rabbi Yehoshua answered, "It is not in heaven." Elijah later told Rabbi Natan that God smiled and said, "My children have triumphed over Me." The Sages burned what Rabbi Eliezer had declared pure and ostracized him. Rabbi Akiva, dressed in black, told him. He wept, crops were struck, and what he looked at burned. Rabban Gamliel nearly drowned until he prayed. Later his wife Imma Shalom, Rabban Gamliel's sister, found him praying face down and said, "You killed my brother"; just then a shofar announced his death.
why: The Gemara brings the story apropos of verbal mistreatment: it ends with Imma Shalom's teaching that the gates of prayer stay open for those who are wronged by words, and the discussion goes on to the verbal mistreatment of converts.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage who stands alone against the Rabbis on the oven and is ostracized.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: He rebukes the walls and rejects the Divine Voice, saying the Torah is not in heaven.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's disciple, who volunteers to tell him of his ostracism.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The head of the Sages who ostracized Rabbi Eliezer; Imma Shalom's brother.

people.name: Imma Shalom
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's wife and Rabban Gamliel's sister, who guards her husband's prayers.

terms.meaning: A voice from Heaven that announces God's view; here the Sages refuse to decide law by it.
Placed under a ban: others must keep their distance, and the person behaves like a mourner.
The posture of a personal supplication prayer said after the main prayer; it is skipped on the New Moon.
A ram's horn; here it is sounded to announce a death.

note: Rav Yosef bar Ḥama used to seize the slaves of people who owed him money and put them to work. His son Rava asked why. He cited Rav Naḥman: a slave is not worth even the bread he eats, so the owners lost nothing. Rava said Rav Naḥman meant idle slaves like his own slave Dari, who only dances among the wine barrels. His father then cited Rav: one who seizes another's slave and works him owes nothing, since the owner is glad the slave keeps working. Rava replied that this holds only when no money is owed; for a creditor it looks like interest. His father said: I retract.
why: The Gemara has just cited Rav Naḥman's ruling that a lender living in his borrower's courtyard must pay rent, so the stay does not look like interest. Rava uses that same ruling to show his father that working a debtor's slaves is the same problem.

people.name: Rav Yosef bar Ḥama
people.about: Rava's father, who seized the slaves of his debtors and made them work for him.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rav Yosef bar Ḥama's son, who questions his father's practice and persuades him to stop.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Sage whose rulings both father and son cite.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage who ruled that one who seizes another's slave and works him is exempt.

people.name: Dari
people.about: Rav Naḥman's slave, who only dances among the wine barrels.

terms.meaning: Jewish law forbids a lender to take any benefit from a borrower beyond the loan itself; even a benefit that only looks like payment for the loan is forbidden.
Jewish law; the binding ruling on a question.

note: A man sold land with a guarantee to compensate the buyer if the seller's creditors ever took it. The buyer asked to be repaid, in that case, from the seller's very best land; the seller refused, wanting to keep it, but promised his other good land. In the end creditors seized the field, and a flood swept away the seller's very best land, leaving the other good land as his best. Rav Pappa thought the seller must still pay from the good land he had promised. Rav Aḥa of Difti asked Ravina why the seller could not say his promise assumed his best land would still exist, and that his good land had now taken its place. The text gives no final ruling.
why: Just before this, Rav Pappa ruled on land set aside to repay a debt. Here he again judges what a specific promise of land for repayment obligates, and his view is challenged.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Sage who thought the seller must keep his promise and pay from his good land.

people.name: Rav Aḥa of Difti
people.about: Sage who argued to Ravina that the seller could refuse.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Sage to whom Rav Aḥa of Difti put his argument.

terms.meaning: Jewish law grades land as best, middle and poorest. Normally a buyer whose land is seized is compensated from the seller's middle-quality land, so a promise of better land matters.
A seller's commitment to repay the buyer if the seller's creditors later seize the land he sold.

note: A group of ice plant dealers took turns baking for one another. One day the others asked one of them to bake when it was not his turn, and he said: in payment for my baking, guard my cloak. Before he came back, the cloak was stolen. Rav Pappa ruled that they must pay for it. The Sages objected that this was guarding while the owner was working for them, which would excuse them, and Rav Pappa was embarrassed. Then it came out that at that time the cloak's owner had been drinking beer, not baking.
why: The discussion is about when guardians are excused because the owner was working for them. The Gemara retells this case to explain Rav Pappa's embarrassment even under the view that carelessness is never excused: baking out of turn made the dealers paid guardians.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Judge who ruled the dealers liable for the stolen cloak.

terms.meaning: A rule that a guardian is not liable for loss if the owner of the item was working for him at the time.
Someone paid, in money or in kind, to guard another's property. A paid guardian must pay for theft or loss, unlike an unpaid one.

note: As young men, Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sat on the ground before the leading Sages, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa. Their sharp questions and answers led the Sages to give them benches. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi's father, protested that they were taking his only fledgling from him, so Rabbi was sent back to the floor; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa had Rabbi Elazar, who had no father to speak for him, sent back too. Rabbi Elazar was offended at being made Rabbi's equal, and from then on he knocked down Rabbi's arguments before he could make them. Rabbi complained to his father, who said: he is a lion son of a lion, and you are a lion son of a fox.
why: Rabbi Elazar's widow has just told Rabbi she did not know whether her husband was greater than him in Torah; the Gemara tells this to show that he was. It also explains why Rabbi named his father among three truly modest people.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Brilliant young scholar, raised to a bench and then sent back to the floor.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; son of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, seated with Rabbi Elazar as a young man.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: Leading Sage and Rabbi's father, who called himself a fox.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa
people.about: Leading Sage who argued that Rabbi Elazar should be sent back to the floor too.

people.name: Jonathan, son of Saul
people.about: Named by Rabbi as modest, for telling David he would be second to him.

terms.meaning: Used alone, this title means Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
A family who led the Sages and, as the Gemara says, seated Hillel at their head and appointed him Nasi over themselves.
The title of the head of the Sages.

note: Rabbi Ḥanina and Rabbi Ḥiyya used to argue over Torah. Rabbi Ḥanina told Rabbi Ḥiyya he was no match for him: if the Torah were ever forgotten, he could restore it by his reasoning alone. Rabbi Ḥiyya answered that he was the one making sure it would never be forgotten. He sows flax, twines nets, hunts deer and feeds their meat to orphans, makes parchment from the hides and writes the five books of the Torah on it. Then he goes to a town, teaches five children one book each and six children one order of the Mishna each, and tells them to teach one another until he comes back.
why: Just before this, a Divine Voice told Reish Lakish that he had studied Torah like Rabbi Ḥiyya but had not spread it as he did. This exchange shows what that spreading looked like, and the discussion goes on praising Rabbi Ḥiyya.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: Sage who boasted he could restore the Torah by his reasoning if it were forgotten.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Sage who made sure the Torah would not be forgotten by teaching children himself.

terms.meaning: The five books of Moses: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy.
The Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law, is divided into six sections called orders.
